content.tldr: Domain Name System (DNS) maps human-readable domain names to IP addresses; without cryptographic validation, legacy UDP DNS is vulnerable to cache poisoning and traffic hijacking.
content.simple_explanation: DNS traditionally operates over unencrypted UDP port 53. Because UDP is stateless and unauthenticated, adversaries can forge DNS responses (DNS cache poisoning / Kaminsky attacks) to redirect users to malicious clones. Attackers also exploit DNS for command-and-control communication and data exfiltration via DNS tunneling. Modern security architectures enforce DNSSEC (cryptographic signature validation of DNS resource records) and DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) to protect user query privacy.
content.real_world_example: A municipal telephone book: if an attacker secretly swaps the telephone number listed for the police station with the number of their own criminal den, callers unknowingly connect directly to the adversary.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: DNSSEC guarantees the authenticity and integrity of DNS records, but does not provide confidentiality: DNSSEC records travel in cleartext. Pairing DNSSEC with DoT/DoH achieves both integrity and query privacy.
